rationale: B wins by being more disciplined with the merchant economics and proof traps. Its angle, "The merchants with the most to gain from Plaid's card bypass are the ones selling big-ticket items," turns the 70% claim into a real reporter assignment instead of a launch gloss. A has stronger range, but it keeps stepping onto landmines like "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" and "competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen," which are exactly the kind of confident extras that get a pitch killed in the first reply.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" is an unsupported superlative. The update says Plaid uses FedNow rails; it does not prove this is FedNow's biggest commercial test.
"competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen" imports competitors not supplied in the update. Card-network bypass is grounded; processor-war framing needs evidence.
"Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes" and "wants to own the payment" add company-history and intent claims without supplied facts or an executive quote.
"The network density is what makes this different from prior A2A attempts" is plausible, but unproven. It also fails to ask whether the 12,000 connected institutions actually support FedNow.
gaps_in_B: "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" states a historical thesis not in the update. Admitting it needs sourcing helps, but the headline still spends facts it does not have.
"FedNow policy/infrastructure-adoption angle ... duplicate" throws away a viable protagonist. FedNow-as-public-infrastructure is not the same story as A2A category momentum.
"furniture, travel, auto, B2B invoicing" are smart examples, but they are inferred verticals. Fine as hypotheses, not as implied launch-market facts.
"Plaid's flat-fee pitch puts a number on what card networks charge merchants" overstates the data. The update gives an "up to 70% lower" claim, not Plaid's actual fee or a card-rate benchmark.
